Untangling complex sentences

Stage 3 · Reading

Sixty-nine days underground

Long sentences, on purpose. The rescue everybody remembers, and the decade nobody reported.

⛏️🚦
1 · Before you read. A famous rescue is retold for years. Which part of the story usually gets left out?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Sixty-nine days underground

Written for this course, from the Encyclopaedia Britannica account of the 2010 Chile mine rescue and contemporary reporting on the San José collapse and its aftermath.

1The San José copper and gold mine, which lies in the Atacama Desert some forty-five kilometres north of Copiapó and which had killed eight workers between 1998 and 2010, was closed in July 2010 after a rock fall cost a miner his leg, was allowed to reopen on the twenty-eighth of that month once corrective measures had been reported — an economic decision as much as a technical one — and collapsed one week later — a sequence that is almost never mentioned in the accounts which made the rescue famous, and which is treated, in most of them, as historical background rather than as the most relevant thing on the page.

2When the main ramp closed at two in the afternoon on 5 August, trapping thirty-three men at a depth of seven hundred metres and five kilometres from the entrance, the group made for the ventilation shafts, which existed precisely so that men could climb out of a blocked mine and which should therefore have settled the matter in an hour; but the ladders required by the safety code were not there, and the men, having found the one route the regulations promised them and having found it unusable, went back down to the refuge to wait.

3For seventeen days nobody above ground knew whether they were alive, and survival in that period depended not on the drilling equipment, which was still being assembled, but on the men themselves, who rationed two days of emergency food across a fortnight and organised, without being asked to, the shifts and the sleeping arrangements that a psychologist would later describe as the reason the mental strain never became unmanageable. Several exploratory boreholes missed the chamber entirely, partly because the mine’s own maps were not reliable; the eighth found it, and came back up with a note attached.

4What followed was impressive by any objective measure: three separate drilling plans running at once, of which the one that broke through was a rig normally used for boring water holes rather than for reaching people; a medical team on site well before the shaft was finished; and, on 13 October, an operation lasting about twenty-two hours which brought every one of the thirty-three to the surface and which an estimated one billion people watched.

5What followed was also, in the way it was told, extremely selective, because the account that reached that billion began on the day the drill arrived rather than in the decade when the warnings were ignored, and a story that begins in the right place is inspiring in a way that a story beginning in the wrong one never is. A congressional commission afterwards placed the blame on the mine’s owners and on the state body that was supposed to inspect them.

6The ending is less tidy than the broadcast. Many of the men were left with lasting physical and mental difficulties, several were unable to work, and the compensation they were awarded — upheld by Chile’s Supreme Court in 2023, at about forty-eight thousand dollars each for the thirty-one who took part in the case — arrived thirteen years after the collapse. It is an unfortunate fact about rescues that the part which is easy to film is also the part that ends.

Text A · Before the drill arrived

Written for this course, from the Encyclopaedia Britannica account of the 2010 Chile mine rescue and contemporary reporting.

The San José copper and gold mine, which lies in the Atacama Desert some forty-five kilometres north of Copiapó and which had killed eight workers between 1998 and 2010, was closed in July 2010 after a rock fall cost a miner his leg, was allowed to reopen on the twenty-eighth of that month once corrective measures had been reported — an economic decision as much as a technical one — and collapsed one week later — a sequence that is almost never mentioned in the accounts which made the rescue famous, and which is treated, in most of them, as historical background rather than as the most relevant thing on the page.

When the main ramp closed at two in the afternoon on 5 August, trapping thirty-three men at a depth of seven hundred metres and five kilometres from the entrance, the group made for the ventilation shafts, which existed precisely so that men could climb out of a blocked mine and which should therefore have settled the matter in an hour; but the ladders required by the safety code were not there, and the men, having found the one route the regulations promised them and having found it unusable, went back down to the refuge to wait.

For seventeen days nobody above ground knew whether they were alive, and survival in that period depended not on the drilling equipment, which was still being assembled, but on the men themselves, who rationed two days of emergency food across a fortnight and organised, without being asked to, the shifts and the sleeping arrangements that a psychologist would later describe as the reason the mental strain never became unmanageable. Several exploratory boreholes missed the chamber entirely, the mine’s own maps having proved less reliable than anyone expected; the eighth found it, and came back up with a note attached.

Text B · Where the telling begins

Written for this course, from contemporary reporting on the rescue and its aftermath.

What followed was impressive by any objective measure: three separate drilling plans running at once, of which the one that broke through was a rig normally used for boring water holes rather than for reaching people; a medical team on site well before the shaft was finished; and, on 13 October, an operation lasting about twenty-two hours which brought every one of the thirty-three to the surface and which an estimated one billion people watched.

What followed was also, in the way it was told, extremely selective, because the account that reached that billion began on the day the drill arrived rather than in the decade when the warnings were ignored, and a story that begins in the right place is inspiring in a way that a story beginning in the wrong one never is. A congressional commission afterwards placed the blame on the mine’s owners and on the state body that was supposed to inspect them, which is a sentence that appeared in far fewer places than the pictures did.

The ending is less tidy than the broadcast. Many of the men were left with lasting physical and mental difficulties, several were unable to work, and the compensation they were awarded — upheld by Chile’s Supreme Court in 2023, at about forty-eight thousand dollars each for the thirty-one who took part in the case — arrived thirteen years after the collapse. It is an unfortunate fact about rescues that the part which is easy to film is also the part that ends, while the medical and economic consequences, which have no obvious final image, continue long after the cameras have been packed away.

1 · Read the explanation.
Reporting inside written English

The rules from lesson 37 still apply. A past reporting verb pulls the reported verb one step back; pronouns and time words shift; reported questions take statement word order and if or whether. What changes in written reports is how often the reporting is invisible.

The passive replaces the reporting verb. Instead of The board rejected the proposal twice, an inquiry writes The proposal had been rejected twice. The action is stated and nobody is named. This is not always evasion — sometimes the agent is genuinely unknown — but it is always worth noticing.

Impersonal reporting. It is said that…, It is thought that…, It is believed that…, He is thought to have left. These attribute a claim to nobody in particular and are extremely common in news writing.

Future from the past. When a text set in the past looks forward, will becomes would: a psychologist would later describe…, the equipment that would arrive eleven days later.

Hedges. Apparently, reportedly, supposedly, allegedly and according to all mark a claim as somebody else’s. Allegedly is the strongest and is used when a crime is involved and nothing has been proved.

The commonest errors at this level
  • According to me — English uses in my view; according to is for other sources.
  • It is said that he would have left where He is thought to have left is meant.
  • Forgetting would for the future seen from the past.
  • Using allegedly for anything that is merely uncertain.
  • Reported questions that keep the inversion: nobody knew were they alive.

Two things to watch

1 — Every passive hides a question. When you read it was decided, ask who decided. When you write it, ask whether you are hiding somebody on purpose.

2 — According to is never used for yourself. Use in my view, I would argue that, it seems to me.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Turning spoken claims into report English

The raw material: a manager says, “We rejected the second shaft in 2004 because it was too expensive, and we will review the decision next year.”

Step 1 — decide whether you vouch for it. You do not, so use a reporting verb that shows it: The company says that… or claims that….

Step 2 — shift the tenses. Rejected → had rejected; will review → would review; next year → the following year.

Step 3 — consider the passive. If the point is the decision rather than who made it: The second shaft had been rejected in 2004 on grounds of cost.

Step 4 — hedge what is unconfirmed. If the 2004 date comes from the company alone: the shaft was apparently rejected in 2004, or according to the company, in 2004.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Attribution without quotation marks

Reports, inquiries and long articles almost never quote. Everything anybody said arrives already reported, and the writer’s job is to make clear who said it and how far they stand behind it.

A statement: The company said that the shaft was safe. A question: Nobody knew whether the men were alive — no inversion, no question mark. The future seen from the past: a psychologist would later describe it as… Attribution with the agent removed — the passive: It had been rejected twice. Attribution to nobody in particular: It is thought that the sensor failed earlier, He is thought to have left early. Attribution to a source: According to the inquiry… Hedges: apparently, reportedly, supposedly, allegedly — The alarm had apparently sounded twice.

Which hedge, and why the tense matters

The hedges are not interchangeable. Apparently is everyday and means ‘so it seems’. Reportedly attributes to reports you are not vouching for. Supposedly leans towards doubt. Allegedly is the legal one: it marks an accusation that has not been proved, and in writing about a crime it is not optional. He allegedly took the money and He took the money expose a publisher to entirely different consequences.

Tense carries meaning too. He has never been named (present perfect passive) says the situation still holds today; He was never named closes it in the past. In an inquiry report that difference is the difference between an open question and a finished one.

And note what the passive is doing. It had been rejected twice removes whoever rejected it. That is fair when the person is unknown or irrelevant, and evasive when the writer knows perfectly well. A careful reader asks, every time, who has gone missing from the sentence.

Errors to watch: Nobody knew were the men alive → whether the men were alive · It is thought that failed → a subject is needed · According to the inquiry says that → According to the inquiry,… · He was allegedly took it → He allegedly took it.

1 · Read the model.
Model · an account in four paragraphs

The bridge that collapsed in March had been inspected eleven times in twelve years, and the report that followed each inspection recommended, in language that grew slightly firmer each time, the replacement of four bearings that were never replaced. That is the fact from which everything else follows, although the coverage in March began, as such coverage does, at eight minutes past six on the morning it fell.

What is known is this. Nobody was on the bridge; the closure at five that morning had been ordered by a duty engineer who has still not been named and who is believed to have acted on a phone call from a driver rather than on any instrument. The city says the closure was routine. According to the driver, whose account was published a week later, he had reported a noise he could not describe.

What is not known is why the bearings were not replaced. It is thought that the money was moved to a road project in 2019, but the relevant minutes have apparently not survived, and the two officials who would be able to explain the decision have both left. An objective account of that year is not yet possible.

The version that circulated in March was accurate and extremely selective: an empty bridge, a lucky closure, an inspiring engineer. Everything in it is true. What it leaves out is eleven inspections and four bearings, and those, not the eight minutes past six, are the story.
